name: Qin Dynasty
summary: The first unified Chinese empire. Qin Shi Huang standardised writing, money and measures, but the dynasty collapsed only 15 years after unification.

knownFor.label: Terracotta Army
knownFor.note: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers guarding the first emperor’s tomb.

knownFor.label: Standardised script & coins
knownFor.note: One writing system, currency and set of measures for all China.

knownFor.label: Great Wall (early)
knownFor.note: Earlier walls joined into a long northern defence.

location.value: Rose from the Guanzhong basin (the Wei River valley, around modern Xi’an) and unified all of China proper by 221 BCE.

terrain.value: The fertile Guanzhong basin, protected by mountains and passes. A Han-era saying runs: “Guanzhong produces generals, while Guandong produces ministers.”

climate.value: Temperate, monsoon-influenced. Droughts and eclipses were read as omens.

resources.value: Irrigated grain land (millet, wheat, barley), boosted by the Zheng Guo canal (246 BCE).

disasters.value: No floods, famines or epidemics are documented in the sources checked.

population.value: Not stated in the Wikipedia article. Most estimates for unified China around 210 BCE fall in the tens of millions. Commoners and villagers made up more than 90% of the population.

urbanisation.value: The capital Xianyang was built on the Wei River. Defeated states’ elites were moved there.

disease.value: No epidemics are documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Over 100,000 prisoners and exiles were moved to colonise newly conquered southern lands.

economicBase.value: Cereal agriculture (millet, wheat, barley). The state promoted farming and war and distrusted commerce.

tradeRoutes.value: A national road system and canals, including the Lingqu canal supporting southern campaigns, connected the empire.

wealth.value: No estimate of total economic output or wealth is given in the sources checked. Commoners made up more than 90% of the population.

moneyAndTax.value: Standardised bronze Ban Liang coins, the first uniform currency across China. Private minting was banned. Weights and measures were standardised.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Qin dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); Wikipedia: Qin Shi Huang (checked 5 Nov 2026)

inequality.value: A merit-based system of twenty military ranks rewarded soldiers with land, houses and slaves. Merchants were heavily restricted (a 214 BCE law let them be drafted and deported).

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy with a centralised bureaucracy run on Legalist principles (Han Fei, Shang Yang).

keyRulers.value: Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor (king of Qin from 246 BCE, emperor 221–210 BCE). Qin Er Shi (210–207 BCE). Chancellors Li Si and Zhao Gao.

succession.value: On Qin Shi Huang’s death in 210 BCE, Zhao Gao and Li Si hid the news and forged an order for the heir Fusu to kill himself, putting Huhai (Qin Er Shi) on the throne.

institutions.value: 36 commanderies and over 1,000 counties replaced feudal fiefs. A Censorate. Standardised writing, money and measures. Strict written laws.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Qin dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

stability.value: Popular revolts broke out within a year of the first emperor’s death (Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, 209 BCE), spreading across the empire.

eliteConflict.value: Court intrigue after 210 BCE. Zhao Gao had Li Si executed (208 BCE) and later forced Qin Er Shi to suicide.

armyAndTech.value: Mass conscript armies organised by Shang Yang’s reforms, with ranks rewarded for enemies killed. About 500,000 troops were reportedly sent south against the Baiyue (214 BCE).

majorWars.value: Wars of unification, 230–221 BCE: Han (230), Zhao (228), Yan (226), Wei (225), Chu (223) and Qi (221). General Meng Tian’s campaign against the Xiongnu (215 BCE). The southern campaigns against the Baiyue.

territoryChange.value: About 2.3 million km² by 220 BCE (Wikipedia infobox). Expanded into the Ordos region and the far south (Guangzhou, Guilin).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were the six Warring States (Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan, Qi), the Xiongnu, and the Baiyue peoples of the south.

inventions.value: Standardised axles, weapons and measures. Huge state projects: the northern walls (forerunner of the Great Wall), national roads, canals, and the first emperor’s mausoleum.

scienceEducation.value: Small seal script was standardised. Tradition says books were burned and scholars buried in 213–212 BCE, but this account (first recorded in the Shiji, c. 91 BCE) is disputed.

openness.value: Recruited talented officials from rival states (e.g. Li Si from Chu, Shang Yang from Wei). Intellectual diversity was suppressed in favour of Legalism.

communicationTransport.value: Standardised measurements, including chariot axle length; a national road system; the Wei River canal (246 BC).

religion.value: Worship of spirits and ancestors, divination, and imperial tours to sacred mountains. The first emperor sought immortality.

languageWriting.value: A unified writing system (small seal script) across the empire, a key and lasting legacy.

artsArchitecture.value: The Terracotta Army (discovered 1974), buried with Qin Shi Huang near Xi’an. Stone inscriptions and palaces at Xianyang.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Qin dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

socialStructure.value: Mostly farming households. Twenty merit ranks. Convicts and slaves did forced labour. Professions were often hereditary.

sharedIdentity.value: A unified script, coinage and law laid the foundation of a single Chinese state. The name “China” may come from “Qin”, but this is questioned.

dailyLife.value: Millet, wheat and barley were the staple crops; hundreds of thousands of peasants and convicts worked on walls, roads and construction.

neighbours.value: The Xiongnu to the north, the Baiyue to the south, and Central Asian peoples to the west.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Legalist administration and the unified script, which the Han inherited and softened.

colonisation.value: Colonised the south with soldiers, convicts and settlers. Historians debate how far real administrative control reached south of the Yangtze.

riseSignals.value: Shang Yang’s administrative and military reforms (359–338 BCE), a protected and fertile homeland, merit-based ranks, and recruitment of talent from rival states.

peakPeriod.value: Unification in 221 BCE, when King Ying Zheng declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the “first emperor”.

declineSignals.value: Harsh laws and heavy labour demands (walls, roads, tombs), a succession plot after 210 BCE, executions and rising taxes under Qin Er Shi, and revolts from 209 BCE.

outcome.value: Collapse. Ziying surrendered to Liu Bang in 207 BCE, and Xiang Yu destroyed Xianyang in 206 BCE. Liu Bang founded the Han, which kept most Qin institutions.

sources.value: The Shiji (Sima Qian, c. 91 BCE), excavated Qin legal texts (Shuihudi bamboo slips), and archaeology (the mausoleum and Terracotta Army). Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Lewis (2007).

overallCertainty.value: Good for the main events. The end date appears as 207 or 206 BCE in different sources. Some famous stories (the book burning, details of the succession plot) come from Han-era historians who were hostile to the Qin.
